7. No evidence was adduced by the defence. 

 8. After considering the evidence adduced by the prosecution the learned Special Tribunal found that the appellant was in possession and control of the fire-arm and ammunition in question without any licence issued under the provision of the Arms Act for possessing the same and, as such, convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid by his judgment dated 6.8.88. 

 10. Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has attacked the finding of the learned Special Tribunal on the ground that two of the local inhabitants who were witnesses for the prosecution and who were also witnesses in the seizure list stated that they were not present when the search and seizure were made by PW2 Md. Asaduzzaman, that they were called at the house of the appellant from their respective houses and were asked to put their signatures on the seizure list and, as such, the search and seizure not being in accordance with section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the learned Special Tribunal should have left the evidence relating to the above alleged search and recovery of the fire-arm, and preparation of the seizure list along with the seizure list itself out of consideration. Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury has further contended that if these facts were left out of consideration the allegation about possession of the incriminating fire-arm and the incriminating ammunition by the appellant could not be said to have been proved and the appellant was, therefore, entitled to be acquitted. 

 16. It is therefore, patent from the evidence of the above witnesses that except the police personnel namely, PW 2, PW 3, PW 4, PW 5, PW 6, and PW 9, the two local inhabitant witnesses namely, PW 8 and PW 10 did not see the appellant to produce the fire-arm and the ammunition and it is also patent that the search and seizure did not take place in their presence. The evidence of the above two local inhabitants proved that after the search and alleged recovery of the fire-arm had been over these two witnesses were called in and they then signed the seizure list. There is no doubt that the Police personnel’s who were alleged to have conducted the search and seizure were interested witnesses and, as such, in a case of this nature, evidence of impartial and independent witnesses is necessary in order to at least lend corroboration to the evidence of the police personnel’s regarding search and seizure of incriminating articles. 

 17. In addition, Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury has referred to section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which reads as follows: 

 "103 (1) Before making a search under this Chapter, the officer or other person about to make it shall call upon two or more respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situate to attend and witness the search and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do. 

 18. From a plain reading of sub-section (1) of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure it is abundantly clear that the search by the police must be conducted in presence of at least two respectable inhabitants of the locality and the things which are to be seized in connection with any case are to be seized during the course of such search conducted in presence of at least two respectable local inhabitants. The requirements of sub-section (2) of section 103 read with sub-section (1) of section 103 are that the entire search from the beginning to the end must be conducted in presence of two respectable local inhabitants and the requirements are not fulfilled if the search and the seizure have taken place either preceding the arrival of the local inhabitants or takes place after their departure from the place of search. The provision relating to search and seizure provided in sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are mandatory and any search and seizure without strictly complying with the aforesaid provisions must be deemed to be illegal and, as such, must be left out of consideration in a criminal trial. 

 19. From the evidence of PWs 8 and 10 it is clear that the search had taken place and the seizure of the fire-arm and the ammunition had been made before their arrival at the place of occurrence and in their absence. As such, the search as well as the seizure of the fire-arm and the ammunition including the preparation of the seizure list by PW2 Md Azaduzzaman and marked Ext. 2 before the learned Special Tribunal were illegal Consequently, the learned Special Tribunal could not have considered the evidence relating to the search and seizure of the fire-arm and the ammunition as well as the seizure list Ext. 2 for arriving at the finding regarding the possession of the said fire-arm and ammunition. If the seizure list Ext. 2 and the evidence relating to recovery of the fire-arm from the possession of the appellant were left out of consideration there was no material before the learned Special Tribunal to hold that the prosecution was able to prove that the incriminating fire-arm and the ammunition were found in possession of the appellant on the date of occurrence. As such, from this point of view also the appellant was entitled to acquittal as the prosecution had not been able to prove its case before the learned Special Tribunal beyond all reasonable doubt.
